references.text: Moses uses the same argument that the Egyptians will hear about it and speak negatively of the Lord's actions if he destroys his people.
Moses refers to the same concern that the people in the land they left will say the Lord brought them out to kill them.
The same fear of enemies misinterpreting God's actions toward His people.
Joshua expresses similar concern about what the nations will say regarding God's name.
The following verse shows that the Lord relented from the disaster He had planned to bring, in response to Moses' prayer.
Jonah refers to God's ability to relent from the disaster He had planned.
Joel calls for repentance with the hope that God will turn from His anger and relent.
The Lord relented from the disaster He had threatened against Judah during King Hezekiah's time.
The psalmist affirms that God relents according to His great mercy.
Background for the exodus from Egypt through the wilderness, which Moses refers to in his prayer.
Highlights the connection between God's willingness to relent from judgment through intercession (Exodus) and the inevitable disaster that occurs when the people refuse to repent (2 Chronicles).
Contrasts Moses' prayer to stop the disaster with Solomon's explanation of why disaster comes when God's people turn away from Him.
Direct theological parallel: Both verses illustrate the principle that God's planned disaster can be averted if the people repent.
